issues.legal_issue: A pending civil eviction suit concerning a non-residential building formerly exempt from rent control abates when the building is brought within rent control, even if the plaint does not expressly plead the exemption.
material_facts: A landlord sued in a civil court for possession and damages after terminating the tenancy of a non-residential building that had been exempt from rent control.
While the suit was pending, an amendment withdrew the exemption and brought the building within the rent-control regime.
The plaint did not expressly state that the suit was brought because the building was exempt, but the requested civil-court relief depended on that exemption.
issues.conclusion: The suit was a proceeding instituted in the light of the former exemption and abated when the amendment took effect; an express allegation of exemption in the plaint was unnecessary.
issues.legal_principle: The abatement provision in section 3 of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Amendment Act, 1964 must be construed in its statutory context and in light of its purpose of protecting tenants in buildings newly brought within the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960. A proceeding is within the provision when it was instituted in the light of the exemption in section 30(iii), even if the plaint does not expressly mention that clause. Without the exemption, section 10 of the principal Act prevented an effective civil-court decree for eviction. P. J. Gupta & Co. v. K. Venkatesan Merchant did not determine which kinds of proceeding fell within the abatement provision, but recognized that a pending proceeding instituted on the ground of exemption would abate.

rule.if: pending_civil_eviction_suit and nonresidential_building_previously_exempt and building_brought_under_rent_control and civil_relief_depended_on_exemption

predicates.pending_civil_eviction_suit: A landlord had a civil-court eviction suit pending when the relevant legal change took effect.
predicates.nonresidential_building_previously_exemp: The property in the pending suit was a non-residential building previously excluded from rent-control protections.
predicates.building_brought_under_rent_control: A legal change brought the building within the rent-control regime while the suit was pending.
predicates.civil_relief_depended_on_exemption: The landlord sought civil-court relief that could not have been effectively granted under the rent-control regime.

issues.definition: When a pending civil eviction suit concerns a formerly exempt non-residential building newly brought under rent control and the requested civil relief depended on the exemption, the suit abates.

issues.legal_issue: A former tenant who remains in a previously leased non-residential building after termination of the lease may receive statutory tenant protection when the building becomes subject to rent control.
material_facts: The original occupant had leased the non-residential building and remained in possession after the lease was terminated.
The building had been leased for commercial use and became subject to rent control after the exemption for such buildings was removed.
The civil eviction suit abated when the amended rent-control regime took effect.
issues.conclusion: The original occupant was not a trespasser after the amendment took effect; he became a statutory tenant and could be evicted only through the procedure prescribed by the rent-control law. The building remained a building within the statutory definition despite termination of the lease and the absence of an intention to relet it.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(2) and 2(8) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 must be read in context: a building previously leased and still occupied after termination of the tenancy can remain a building, and a person continuing in possession after termination can be a tenant. Sections 10 and 14 to 16 prescribe the applicable eviction process. Section 3 of the 1964 Amending Act brought the building under the principal Act. The Court relied on the reasoning in Moolchand Gupta v. Madras Piece Goods Merchants Charitable Trust concerning the status of an occupant who remains in possession after termination, and on R. K. Veerappa Naidu v. N. Gopalan in construing a building 'to be let.'

rule.if: pending_eviction_dispute and former_lease_occupant_remains and previously_leased_nonresidential_building and building_brought_under_rent_control

predicates.pending_eviction_dispute: A dispute concerns eviction of an occupant from a building when rent-control protection becomes applicable.
predicates.former_lease_occupant_remains: A person who occupied under a lease continues to possess the premises after the lease is terminated.
predicates.previously_leased_nonresidential_buildin: The premises are a non-residential building that was previously leased for use by an occupant.
predicates.building_brought_under_rent_control: A legal change brings the previously leased building within rent-control protections.

issues.definition: A former lease occupant who remains in a previously leased non-residential building receives statutory tenant protection when that building becomes subject to rent control.

issues.legal_issue: A proceeding that has abated by operation of law cannot later be revived or amended to add parties and a new cause of action.
material_facts: The civil eviction suit abated when the building became subject to rent control.
The original defendant died after the suit had abated.
The landlord later amended the plaint to seek relief against newly added parties on a cause of action arising after the original defendant's death.
The courts below treated the matter as a live suit and entered a decree against the added parties.
issues.conclusion: The later addition of parties and amendment of the plaint were without jurisdiction, and the decrees against the added parties were unsustainable. The suit was disposed of as having abated, while the questions concerning the added parties' entitlement to protection were left open for appropriate proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: A plaint may be amended to add parties or relief only while a suit is pending in law. Once section 3 of the 1964 Amending Act caused the suit to abate, no live proceeding remained to amend or convert into a fresh suit. Parties cannot confer jurisdiction by consent or acquiescence. B. Banerjee v. Anita Pan was inapplicable because there was no comparable statutory impediment to continuing proceedings in that case.

predicates.civil_eviction_suit_abated: A civil eviction suit ended by operation of law before the later proceedings occurred.
predicates.later_parties_added: The claimant subsequently sought relief against persons who were not parties to the suit before it ended.
predicates.later_cause_of_action_claimed: The later claim against the added parties relied on a cause of action arising after the original suit had ended.

issues.definition: When a civil eviction suit has abated before new parties and a later cause of action are introduced, the amendment and resulting decree are without jurisdiction.

issues.legal_issue: A coordinate bench that cannot distinguish an earlier decision of a coordinate bench and considers it wrong should refer the issue to a larger bench rather than disregard the earlier decision.
material_facts: An earlier decision of a division bench of the same High Court addressed the legal status of an occupant who remained in possession after termination of a tenancy.
A later division bench considered the earlier decision inapplicable because a particular argument had not been addressed in it, and proceeded without referring the issue to a larger bench.
issues.conclusion: The later division bench should have referred the matter to a larger bench rather than bypassing the earlier decision.
issues.legal_principle: Judicial decorum and legal certainty require a coordinate bench that disagrees with an earlier decision of the same court, and cannot distinguish it, to refer the issue to a larger bench. The Court relied on Smt. Sommavanti v. State of Punjab regarding the binding effect of a decision and Mahadeolal Kanodia v. Administrator-General of West Bengal regarding the proper procedure for addressing disagreement with a coordinate-bench decision.

predicates.coordinate_bench_proceeding: A case is being considered by a bench of the same court with authority coordinate to an earlier bench.
predicates.earlier_coordinate_decision_on_issue: An earlier coordinate bench has decided the legal issue presented in the later case.
predicates.later_bench_cannot_distinguish_and_disag: The later bench considers the earlier decision wrong but cannot distinguish it on the issue before it.

issues.definition: When a coordinate bench encounters an indistinguishable earlier coordinate decision with which it disagrees, the issue must be referred to a larger bench.
